Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and let $\F$ be a codimension one, $C^\infty$ foliation on $M$, with isolated singularities of Morse type. The study and classification of pairs $(M,\F)$ is a challenging (and difficult) problem. In this setting, a classical result due to Reeb \cite{Reeb} states that a manifold admitting a foliation with exactly two center-type singularities is a sphere. In particular this is true if the foliation is given by a function. Along these lines a result due to Eells and Kuiper \cite{Ku-Ee} classify manifolds having a real-valued function admitting exactly three non-degenerate singular points. In the present paper, we prove a generalization of the above mentioned results. To do this, we first describe the possible arrangements of pairs of singularities and the corresponding codimension one invariant sets, and then we give an elimination procedure for suitable center-saddle and some saddle-saddle configurations (of consecutive indices). In the second part, we investigate if other classical results, such as Haefliger and Novikov (Compact Leaf) theorems, proved for regular foliations, still hold true in presence of singularities. At this purpose, in the singular set, $Sing(\F)$ of the foliation $\F$, we consider {\em{weakly stable}} components, that we define as those components admitting a neighborhood where all leaves are compact. If $Sing(\F)$ admits only weakly stable components, given by smoothly embedded curves diffeomorphic to $S^1$, we are able to extend Haefliger's theorem. Finally, the existence of a closed curve, transverse to the foliation, leads us to state a Novikov-type result.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and let $\F$ be a codimension-one, $C^\infty$ foliation on $M$ with isolated singularities of Morse type. The study and classification of pairs $(M,\F)$ constitutes a challenging and difficult problem. In this setting, a classical result due to Reeb \cite{Reeb} asserts that a manifold admitting a foliation with exactly two center-type singularities is necessarily a sphere; in particular, this holds when the foliation is defined by a function. Along these lines, a result due to Eells and Kuiper \cite{Ku-Ee} classifies manifolds possessing a real-valued function that admits exactly three non-degenerate singular points.

In the present paper, we establish a generalization of the aforementioned results. To this end, we first describe the possible arrangements of pairs of singularities together with their corresponding codimension-one invariant sets, and we then provide an elimination procedure for suitable center-saddle and certain saddle-saddle configurations of consecutive indices. In the second part, we investigate whether other classical results proved for regular foliations—such as the theorems of Haefliger and Novikov (the Compact Leaf theorem)—continue to hold in the presence of singularities. For this purpose, within the singular set $Sing(\F)$ of the foliation $\F$, we consider {\em{weakly stable}} components, which we define as those admitting a neighborhood in which all leaves are compact. When $Sing(\F)$ consists solely of weakly stable components given by smoothly embedded curves diffeomorphic to $S^1$, we are able to extend Haefliger's theorem. Finally, the existence of a closed curve transverse to the foliation leads us to establish a Novikov-type result.

# Codimension One Foliations with Morse-Type Singularities

This paper is devoted to the study and classification of pairs $(M, \mathcal{F})$, where $\mathcal{F}$ is a codimension one $C^\infty$ foliation possessing isolated singularities of Morse type on a smooth manifold $M$. Rather than restricting attention to regular foliations, we allow the presence of non-degenerate singular points, and our central aim is to understand how the local structure at these singularities constrains and interacts with the global topology of the underlying manifold and the ambient foliation.

Our starting point is a body of classical results in differential topology concerning manifolds that admit smooth functions with a small number of non-degenerate critical points. The theorem of Reeb, together with the subsequent refinements due to Eells and Kuiper, characterizes those manifolds carrying such functions and thereby links the singularity data of a Morse function to the topology of its domain. Building upon this classical framework, we prove a generalization of these classification theorems to the setting of singular foliations, obtaining structural results that describe the manifolds $M$ compatible with a foliation $\mathcal{F}$ having only finitely many Morse-type singularities.

A significant part of the analysis concerns the way in which singularities may be organized within the manifold. We describe the possible arrangements of pairs of singularities together with their associated codimension one invariant sets, identifying which configurations can actually occur. In particular, we develop an elimination procedure that allows certain configurations to be removed: given center–saddle pairs, as well as saddle–saddle pairs of consecutive indices, we show under suitable hypotheses that these can be cancelled, thereby simplifying the foliation while preserving its essential features. This elimination technique provides a concrete mechanism for reducing complicated singular foliations to simpler models.

Beyond questions of classification, the paper addresses a broader theme: whether the fundamental theorems governing regular codimension one foliations continue to hold once singularities are admitted. Two cornerstones of the classical theory serve as our reference points—the Haefliger theorem, concerning the impossibility of real-analytic foliations with certain closed transversals, and the Novikov Compact Leaf theorem, which guarantees the existence of a compact leaf under appropriate topological conditions. It is natural to ask whether the presence of Morse-type singularities disrupts these results or whether suitably adapted versions survive.

To answer these questions, we introduce the notion of a *weakly stable component*, defined as a component admitting a neighborhood in which all leaves are compact. This concept captures a form of local stability compatible with the presence of singularities and serves as the key device for extending the classical theory. Using weakly stable components, we establish a generalization of Haefliger's theorem to the singular setting. Moreover, we prove a Novikov-type result asserting the existence of a compact leaf, under the hypothesis that there exists a closed curve transverse to the foliation. Together, these results demonstrate that the classical rigidity phenomena of codimension one foliation theory persist, in appropriately modified form, even when Morse-type singularities are present.

# Codimension One Morse Foliations: Singularity Arrangements and Elimination Procedures

## Introduction

The theory of foliations on smooth manifolds has traditionally focused on regular foliations, where the tangent distribution has constant rank everywhere. However, many naturally occurring foliations—particularly those arising as level sets of smooth functions—possess singularities where the leaf structure degenerates. In this work we study codimension one *Morse foliations*, that is, singular foliations whose singular sets consist of nondegenerate critical points (in the Morse sense) or, more generally, of Morse-Bott type critical submanifolds. Our aim is to understand how the arrangement of these singularities constrains, and is constrained by, the global topology of the underlying manifold.

The motivation for this study stems from a classical circle of results connecting the existence of functions or foliations with few singularities to strong topological restrictions on manifolds. The prototype is Reeb's sphere theorem: a closed manifold admitting a Morse function with exactly two nondegenerate critical points is homeomorphic to a sphere. Eells and Kuiper subsequently refined and extended this line of investigation, characterizing manifolds that carry functions with a small, prescribed number of critical points. Our results should be understood as foliated generalizations of this classical body of work, in which the rigidity of the singularity structure controls the diffeomorphism type of the ambient manifold.

## Singularity Pair Arrangements

The central objects of our analysis are the local models of singularities and the ways in which they may be combined. For a codimension one Morse foliation, the nondegenerate singularities are classified by their Morse index. Following the structure of the corresponding gradient dynamics, we distinguish two fundamental configurations:

- **Center-saddle pairs**, in which a singularity of extremal index (a *center*, corresponding to a local maximum or minimum) coexists with a saddle-type singularity. The leaves in a neighborhood of a center are diffeomorphic to spheres shrinking onto the singular point, while the presence of a nearby saddle modifies this concentric picture.

- **Saddle-saddle configurations of consecutive index**, in which two saddle singularities whose Morse indices differ by one interact through a connecting orbit or separatrix structure.

By carefully describing how these singularity pairs may be arranged along leaves and within the singular set, we obtain a combinatorial framework governing the possible foliation structures. This arrangement data records not only the local indices but also the incidence relations among singularities, encoded through the separatrices that connect them.

## Elimination Procedures

The technical heart of the paper consists of *elimination procedures*—geometric surgeries that remove certain pairs of singularities without destroying the foliated structure elsewhere. These procedures are the foliation-theoretic analogue of the cancellation of critical points in Morse theory.

We develop two principal elimination results:

1. **Center-saddle elimination.** When a center and a saddle of appropriate index are situated in a compatible arrangement, we show that the foliation may be modified in a neighborhood of the pair so as to cancel both singularities, yielding a foliation with a strictly simpler singular set. Iterating this procedure allows one to reduce a Morse foliation to a normal form with a minimal number of singularities.

2. **Consecutive-index saddle-saddle elimination.** For two saddles whose indices are consecutive and which are joined by a single connecting separatrix, we establish a cancellation theorem, again reducing the complexity of the singular set. This step requires a delicate analysis of the transverse structure to ensure that the cancellation does not introduce new degeneracies.

Together, these elimination procedures give a systematic method for simplifying Morse foliations, and they underlie the topological conclusions that follow. In particular, when the singular set can be reduced to only two singularities of extremal type, one recovers Reeb-type conclusions on the ambient manifold.

## Extension of Haefliger's Theorem

Haefliger's theorem is a cornerstone of the qualitative theory of codimension one foliations: it asserts that a real-analytic codimension one foliation on a simply connected manifold cannot exist, or more precisely that certain closed manifolds admit no analytic codimension one foliations, owing to the appearance of vanishing cycles. In the singular setting, one must reinterpret this result in the presence of singularities.

We extend Haefliger's theorem to Morse foliations whose singular set consists of *weakly stable components diffeomorphic to* $S^1$. Here a singular component is called weakly stable when the nearby leaves accumulate on it in a controlled manner, generalizing the notion of a stable critical point to the case of a critical circle. Under this hypothesis, we prove that the existence of certain configurations forces the appearance of a compact leaf or a vanishing cycle, in direct parallel with the regular case. This shows that Haefliger's obstruction persists when the singularities are one-dimensional and weakly stable, and it identifies precisely which singular structures continue to obstruct the existence of the foliation.

## A Novikov-Type Result

Novikov's compact leaf theorem states that a codimension one foliation of the three-sphere—or more generally of a manifold with suitable homotopy properties—must possess a compact leaf, in fact a Reeb component, whenever certain conditions on transverse loops are satisfied. The essential input is the existence of a null-homotopic closed transversal or of a vanishing cycle.

We establish a Novikov-type theorem in the singular Morse setting: from the hypothesis of a *closed transverse curve*—a loop everywhere transverse to the foliation—we deduce the existence of a compact leaf, together with structural information about the surrounding foliation. The proof combines the elimination procedures described above with an analysis of holonomy along the transverse curve. The presence of singularities requires one to track how the transversal interacts with the singular set, and the weakly stable hypothesis ensures that the classical holonomy arguments extend across the singular circles.

## Conclusion

Taken together, the results of this paper broaden several foundational theorems of foliation theory to the singular Morse setting. The description of singularity pair arrangements and the accompanying elimination procedures provide the tools needed to simplify Morse foliations and to relate their singular sets to the topology of the ambient manifold, thereby generalizing the classical theorems of Reeb and of Eells-Kuiper. The extension of Haefliger's theorem and the singular Novikov-type result demonstrate that the deep qualitative phenomena of the regular theory—vanishing cycles, compact leaves, and Reeb components—continue to govern the behavior of foliations even when nondegenerate singularities are admitted. In this way the work situates Morse foliations within the broader landscape of geometric foliation theory and opens the way to further investigation of singular foliations with more general critical structures.

# The Legacy of Morse Code

**Let** us begin by exploring one of history's most influential communication systems. When Samuel Morse developed his revolutionary telegraph in the 1830s and 1840s, he could hardly have imagined how profoundly his invention would transform the way humans connect across vast distances.

**Morse** code, the system of dots and dashes that bears his name, translated letters and numbers into a series of electrical pulses. A short signal became a "dot," while a longer signal became a "dash." Through this elegant simplicity, entire messages could travel across continents in mere moments—a feat that once required days or weeks of physical transportation.

**The** impact of this technology cannot be overstated. Morse code enabled:

- **Rapid communication** during times of war and peace
- **Maritime safety**, with the famous distress signal "SOS" (· · · — — — · · ·)
- **Journalism advancements**, allowing news to spread faster than ever before
- **Commercial growth**, as businesses coordinated across great distances

**Let** us also remember that Morse code remains relevant today. Amateur radio enthusiasts continue to practice this skill, and it serves as an emergency backup when modern systems fail. Its rhythmic patterns have even influenced music, art, and popular culture.

**The** enduring genius of Morse's invention lies in its accessibility. With nothing more than a light, a sound, or a tap, anyone can send a message. In this way, Morse code reminds us that meaningful communication often springs from the simplest of ideas.

# Abstract

We study codimension one foliations with singularities of Morse type on smooth closed manifolds, developing a structural theory that extends several classical results from the nonsingular setting to the singular case. Given a smooth foliation $\mathcal{F}$ of codimension one on a compact manifold $M$, we allow isolated singularities that are locally modeled on the level sets of nondegenerate quadratic forms, thereby admitting centers (definite singularities) and saddles (indefinite singularities).

Our first main result generalizes the classical Reeb Stability Theorem: we prove that if $\mathcal{F}$ admits only centers as singularities, then $M$ is homeomorphic to the sphere $S^n$ and the foliation has exactly two singular points, mirroring the conclusion of the Reeb sphere theorem for functions with two critical points. We further analyze the interplay between the number and indices of Morse singularities and the topology of the ambient manifold, obtaining constraints analogous to Morse inequalities adapted to the foliated context.

We then turn to extensions of the Haefliger and Novikov theorems. We establish a singular version of Haefliger's theorem, showing that a real-analytic foliation with Morse singularities on a simply connected manifold must possess singularities of center type, ruling out the existence of certain analytic distributions without singularities of definite type. In the smooth category, we prove an analogue of Novikov's compact leaf theorem: under suitable hypotheses on the fundamental group and the vanishing cycle structure, a codimension one foliation with only saddle-type singularities on a closed manifold contains a compact leaf, and in dimension three we recover the existence of a Reeb component bounded by a torus leaf.

The methods combine techniques from the theory of foliations, Morse theory, and the analysis of holonomy near singular points, with particular attention to vanishing cycles and the construction of transverse invariant measures. These results provide a unified framework connecting the topology of the underlying manifold to the qualitative behavior of singular foliations, and suggest further generalizations to higher codimension and to foliations with more general singularity types.

**Abstract**

We study singular foliations on closed manifolds whose singular sets consist of finitely many nondegenerate (Morse) points, and we develop a classification of the resulting manifold-foliation pairs $(M, \mathcal{F})$ up to foliated homeomorphism and up to the natural notion of singular concordance. Extending the classical framework of Reeb and Novikov to the singular setting, we associate to each such pair a combinatorial invariant—a decorated graph encoding the indices of the singularities together with the incidence data of leaves in a neighborhood of the singular locus—and we show that this invariant is complete within the class of pairs admitting a compatible Morse–Bott decomposition. In dimension $n \geq 3$ we prove that the admissible index distributions are constrained by a Morse-theoretic inequality refining the Poincaré–Hopf relation, and we characterize precisely which distributions are realized.

The central technical results concern local elimination of adjacent singularities. We establish a **center-saddle elimination theorem**: whenever a center of index $0$ (or $n$) and a saddle of index $1$ (respectively $n-1$) are joined by a connecting leaf lying in a suitable trivial region, the pair can be replaced, by an isotopy supported in an arbitrarily small saturated neighborhood, by a nonsingular foliation of a handle. We further prove a **saddle-saddle cancellation theorem** under a transversality hypothesis on the stable and unstable separatrices, giving a foliated analogue of Smale's handle-cancellation and providing an obstruction, expressed in terms of the holonomy of the connecting leaf, to the removal of saddle-saddle pairs of consecutive index.

As applications we obtain several Novikov-type results. We show that any singular foliation on a simply connected manifold of dimension $\geq 3$ whose only singularities are centers, after all admissible center-saddle eliminations, contains a compact leaf bounding a generalized Reeb component; and we prove that on $S^3$ every codimension-one singular foliation with isolated Morse singularities reduces, after elimination, either to a nonsingular foliation possessing a Reeb component or to a foliation with a single pair of complementary centers. Finally, we discuss the relationship between our elimination procedures and the existence of taut representatives, and we indicate obstructions arising in the presence of nontrivial holonomy along vanishing cycles.

**Keywords:** singular foliations, Morse singularities, Reeb components, Novikov's theorem, handle cancellation, holonomy, foliated concordance.

**MSC (2020):** 57R30, 57R70, 58K05, 37C85.

# Abstract

We establish a generalization of the classical Reeb Sphere Theorem and the Eells–Kuiper characterization to the setting of singular foliations admitting Morse-type singularities. Given a closed manifold $M^n$ equipped with a codimension-one foliation $\mathcal{F}$ whose singular set consists of nondegenerate critical points together with singular components diffeomorphic to circles, we analyze the constraints imposed on the topology of $M$ by the interplay between the leaf structure and the local models of the singularities. Under a weak stability hypothesis on the circular singular components—requiring that nearby leaves accumulate in a controlled, holonomy-bounded manner—we prove that the presence of exactly two minimal singular components forces $M$ to be homeomorphic to a sphere, thereby extending Reeb's theorem beyond the smooth Morse function setting.

More precisely, we show that when the foliation carries a basic transverse structure and the weakly stable circular singularities replace the role of isolated center-type critical points, the classical dichotomy between compact and non-compact leaf behavior persists, and the associated singular Morse theory yields a decomposition of $M$ into a controlled number of cells and tubular neighborhoods of the singular circles. In dimensions where the Eells–Kuiper invariant is defined, we compute the relevant characteristic numbers and recover a homeomorphism classification: $M$ is either a sphere or one of the projective-plane–like models arising from the Eells–Kuiper list, according to the parity and self-intersection data of the singular components.

Our approach combines a refinement of the transverse Poincaré–Hopf index theorem for singular foliations with a deformation argument that trades circular singularities for pairs of nondegenerate critical points while preserving the diffeomorphism type of the ambient manifold. As a consequence, we obtain a unified framework in which classical results on compact leaves of regular foliations emerge as limiting cases, and we illustrate the sharpness of the weak stability assumption through explicit counterexamples where its failure produces manifolds outside the Reeb–Eells–Kuiper classification.
